```sql
SELECT pid, backend_type, application_name, state, xact_start
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database()
  AND pid <> pg_backend_pid()
  AND xact_start IS NOT NULL;
```

The query shows who is holding a transaction open. The migration's own gate is still what enforces
the rule. (CodeRabbit full review of PR #843, 2026-09-30.)

**Group-wide date check: the 2026-09-22 measurement** (moved verbatim from the DECISION_LOG entry of
2026-09-22 on 2026-09-30, CodeRabbit on PR #850; the decision itself stays in the log).

**Source:** Mason's decision in this session on 2026-09-22, after two independent adversarial
Claude reviews of PR #762 and a measured PostgreSQL 17 reproduction. Presented as a business
risk trade-off with a recommendation; he chose to keep the stricter guard.

**Background.** CodeRabbit raised a Major on PR #758: `guard_field_app_invoice_season_date()`
PERFORMs the group-wide `_assert_field_app_invoice_date_in_filed_season`, so a single-invoice date
edit inside a mixed-season group is refused whenever another member's season differs, even when the
new date stays inside that invoice's own filed season — stricter than the per-invoice rule recorded
on 2026-09-08 and clarified on 2026-09-13. The relaxation was implemented (row trigger validates
only the written row), reviewed clean by Luna, Sol and CodeRabbit, and then caught by an adversarial
review before merge.

**What was measured** (disposable PostgreSQL 17 container, production shape from the 2026-09-04
accepted consequence: ONE application, ONE group, ONE shared date, member A filed in the EARLIER
season and therefore inconsistent with that shared date):

    A_unchanged_date_group_save         = OK        (the group is usable today)
    single_row_edit_into_A_own_season   = OK        (newly permitted by the relaxation)
    group_save_at_A_date                = REFUSED
    group_save_at_B_date                = REFUSED
    group_save_at_a_third_date          = REFUSED
    converge_A_back_to_B_date           = REFUSED
    converge_B_down_to_A_date           = REFUSED
    preview_group                       = REFUSED

One ordinary, unwarned admin edit leaves the group holding two dates for one physical application.
The field-app save writes ONE date to every member, so every date then fails on one member or the
other, and neither member's date can be moved back because each convergence target lies outside
that member's own filed season. Void-and-reissue becomes the only exit. Before the relaxation that
state was unreachable.

**Decision.** The row trigger KEEPS the group-wide assertion in both `20260914101000` and
`20260914101100`. The relaxation is reverted; both files return to their reviewed bytes and their
original sha256 pins. CodeRabbit's Major is REFUTED with the evidence above rather than implemented.

**Operative rule.** Do not narrow `guard_field_app_invoice_season_date()` to the written row. The
group-wide check is deliberately stricter than the per-invoice date rule: it refuses some edits the
rule would allow, always fail-closed and never with wrong money, in exchange for keeping a
mixed-season group recoverable. The per-invoice rule of 2026-09-08/13 still governs what a date may
be; it does not authorize splitting one group's shared application date. `prove-preview-field-app-season.mjs`
(PHASE 8h-mixed / 8i-mixed) asserts both directions, and its mutant reproduces the stranded state,
so a future attempt fails the proof instead of reaching review.

**Unchanged by this entry:** the 2026-09-04 "invoice season follows the invoice date" decision, the
2026-09-08/13 filed-season rule itself, and the APPLY-WINDOW RULE requiring `20260914101000` and
`20260914101100` to apply in one window.

**Filed-season rule: the 2026-09-08 source and 2026-09-13 clarification** (moved verbatim from the
DECISION_LOG entry of 2026-09-08 on 2026-09-30, CodeRabbit on PR #850).

**Source:** the September 8 continuation of PR #599. Codex's final owner-facing recommendation
was "preserve season immutability but refuse edits that move an existing invoice across the
October 1 season boundary." Mason's next response was "continue 599" (September 8 Chicago /
September 9 UTC). Codex immediately explained that it was continuing with that recommended
rule. This records approval of the preceding recommendation, not a standalone continuation
quote interpreted without its context. Reconciled September 12 after #599 merged without
this follow-up; exact exchange rechecked September 13 during Claude's adversarial review.

**Decision.** Existing field-application invoices keep their filed season. A date can move within
that season but cannot cross its October 1 boundary. Every database writer must also refuse to
change the filed season, preventing a season-first/date-second bypass. New **generic** invoices
still derive season from their invoice date; the dedicated job/blend creators are the documented
exception, qualified in the compatibility clarification immediately below. Preview and save follow
the same rule.

**Compatibility clarification, September 13:** an unchanged stored date is not a date edit.
Dedicated job/blend creators deliberately preserve the source season while stamping today's
date. Those existing invoices must remain usable and restorable at that same stored date,
with their own filed-season pricing. A later changed date must still fit the filed season;
no creator re-seasoning, group-wide price unification, or business-row rewrite is authorized.

This supersedes only the September 4 accepted consequence of editing across October 1 while
adding a grower. It does not re-season existing invoices, unify mixed historical groups, change
the filed-season price lookup, or revive the closed posting-date due-date direction (#591).
The new guard is a separate follow-up to merged #599 and remains unapplied pending live approval.

Migrations are in `supabase/migrations/` ordered by timestamp prefix.
The first column is the historical documentation-entry sequence, not the file
count; one entry can index multiple reconstruction sources restored together.
Sequence reflects entry/landing order, so a migration renamed to its server-assigned
version can have a newer timestamp without changing its documentation sequence.

**Read the number in the title as a high-water sequence, not a row count.**
`scripts/check-doc-drift.mjs` validates it against `max(sequence)` in the table below
and reads only the title form `Migration History (latest entry N)`, which is why the
title reads the way it does. Counted 2026-09-26 with the checker's own row regex, the
table holds **774** parsed rows, 161 fewer than the high-water 935. That gap is the net
of two opposing effects: **751 distinct** sequence numbers are in use, so **184 numbers
between 1 and 935 were never used at all**, while **17 numbers are duplicated**
(286–298, 302, 623, 872, 873) across **23 extra rows**. 184 − 23 = 161, and
774 + 161 = 935. Note the directions differ — skipped numbers raise the high-water
above the row count, duplicates push it back down.
This is also why `check:docs` reports two different totals that both pass: the
`all migrations indexed` row counts `.sql` files in `supabase/migrations/` (927 on
2026-09-26), while `migration-history latest sequence` reads the highest row number here (935).

**These two figures are not interchangeable, and `version` can land on either side of `name`.**
Supabase assigns a fresh `version` at apply time while `name` preserves the authored filename stamp,
so the two drift apart in whichever direction the delay between authoring and applying pushes them.
Both directions are present in this table: in the row above, `20260813080000` was authored 08-13 and
applied 08-16, so its `version` (`20260816174353`) runs **three days ahead** of its `name`; at row 879
below, `20260813070000` was applied the evening of 08-12 and its `version` (`20260813011751`) runs
**behind** its `name`. **The ordering guard derives an effective stamp row by row:** use the timestamp
embedded in that row's `name` when present, otherwise use that row's 14-digit `version` as the
conservative fallback. A bare `max(version)` is never the ordering high-water because it discards
the name context that decides which rows need the fallback. Here the effective maximum comes from
the timestamped `name` `20260813080000`, not its later apply-time version. The 2026-08-16
`migration-drift-reviewer` run read the recorded high-water as stale because it compared a bare
`version` (`20260813011751`) instead of deriving the row's authored stamp from `name`. Row 879 below
records both the `version` (`20260813011751`) and the `name` (`20260813070000`), so the comparison can
be made with the full row context. What this correction changed is the pointer: the sentence used to
cite **row 49**, which is an unrelated 2026-02-17 commission-payments entry (`20260217210000`) and
records neither of those two values.

Scoping on the whole payload loses this to a corrected cost; scoping on the name loses it to a corrected typo. Only a constant survives an arbitrary edit — it took two review rounds to get this right. Because the create op is constant, `saveService()` restricts its rotate-and-retry to the **edit** path; the RPC scoping and the caller rotation are one design and changing either alone reintroduces a bug. The key is **mandatory on create**. Re-scheduled to `20 11 * * *` = **06:20 America/Chicago during CDT** (growing season) / 05:20 during CST — always early morning, never later than 06:20. pg_cron can't track DST, so exact 06:20 year-round isn't possible with a static schedule; the earlier UTC time was chosen to suit early-start ag crews. Cron-reschedule-only (idempotent unschedule+reschedule DO block, byte-identical pattern to u18 lines 557-568); `run_morning_notification_checks()` unchanged. rls + drift reviewers: 0 blockers. Proven live: schedule now `20 11 * * *`, 1 active job, and a rolled-back `PERFORM run_morning_notification_checks()` ran cleanly (370→370, deduped since today's run already fired).

> ➕ **2026-07-10 — A9 close-period guards APPLIED LIVE (live v20260710151913).** `20260711000000_a9_close_period_guards.sql` — Re-emits `close_accounting_period` adding exactly two guards (line-diff of live-vs-new `pg_get_functiondef` inside a rolled-back txn: **0 lines removed, 11 added**). (1) The period must be a whole calendar month — `date_trunc('month', p_period_end)` silently accepted a mid-month end date, and since the unique key is `(period_start, period_end)` a call with `2026-03-15` inserted a **SECOND, overlapping** closed row beside the open full-month row (proven live: `march rows now: 2`), leaving the UI showing March "Open" while its first half was silently locked. NULL is handled explicitly (`NULL <> x` is NULL, which does not RAISE). (2) A period may only be closed **after it has ended** on the **America/Chicago** business clock — previously nothing server-side compared `p_period_end` to the current date at all, so an admin could close the current, in-progress month and block every invoice/payment for the rest of it (proven live: closing `2026-07-31` on 2026-07-10 was ACCEPTED). Guard 2 uses `(now() AT TIME ZONE 'America/Chicago')::date`, **not** `CURRENT_DATE` — the DB session is UTC, so `CURRENT_DATE` runs ~5h ahead of the business day (independent Codex gate P1). Session-tz-immune: with session TimeZone = `Pacific/Kiritimati`, `CURRENT_DATE` = 2026-07-11 but the guard's date stayed 2026-07-10 and July stayed refused. Both guards sit **above** `check_idempotency`, so a cached success can't replay past them. Coupled frontend: `src/lib/dateUtils.ts` gains `BUSINESS_TIMEZONE` + `todayInBusinessTz()`, and `MonthEndClose.tsx` derives `todayStr`, the default period, and the year-option list from it (no `new Date()` remains). rls-security + migration-drift reviewers: 0 blockers. Rolled-back live smoke: July/mid-month/NULL refused, June(ended) falls through to the pre-existing unposted-invoice rule, April(ended, clean) ACCEPTED then refused as already-closed.

  (same leak — verified `confirm_delivery` releases nothing). Body verbatim from live md5

  jsonb (`+prebooked_released`); post-apply md5 `90ba258797cbac40e80673fba0767369`. rls-security +

`20260615173849_backfill_missing_commissions_march_2026` — data-only `DO` block. 11 March-2026 orders (ORD-2026-0148/0150/0153/0161/0162/0177/0178/0179/0180/0186/0188) had no commission rows: they were booked 2026-03-09..03-13, **before** each customer's commission split was configured, so the canonical writer correctly produced nothing at the time. ## Applied 2026-06-11 (idempotency lookup operation-scoping sweep — 20 RPCs)

The C6-control follow-through on the restore_quote_version bug class at scale: 20 live RPCs' inline idempotency LOOKUP filtered only on the key (`WHERE idempotency_key = p_idempotency_key`) with no operation filter, so a cross-operation key collision silently honored another operation's cached row. Each body verbatim-from-live with exactly ONE delta — the lookup gains ` AND operation = '<own name>'` (every INSERT already wrote the correct operation). Drafted in `scripts/.staging-migrations/` per the race guard; section 05 (`create_invoice_from_blend_ticket`) rebased onto the `20260611203238` live body between draft and apply. Both reviewers clean post-rebase (rls 0/0/0, drift 0/0/0); in-transaction self-verify DO block re-asserted all 20 in-database (overload=1, clause exactly once, strip-the-delta md5 == live baseline, SECDEF + search_path, grants posture authenticated+service_role / no anon). Rolled-back smoke `smoke-idempotency_operation_scope_sweep.sql` PASS (`SMOKE_PASS_ROLLBACK`): foreign-operation cached row ignored (call proceeds into the real body), own duplicate honored (cached short-circuit). **Carve-outs (2 of the 22, deliberate):** `create_planned_holds` + `save_quote` excluded — the pending `20260611132115_planned_holds_drawn_sync` (on disk, NOT live) rebuilds both with operation-scoped lookups of its own; sweeping them here would let whichever applied second silently revert the other. Post-apply probe confirms exactly those 2 remain unscoped; they fall off when that migration lands. Builder tooling kept: `scripts/build-idemscope-sweep.mjs` + `scripts/verify-idemscope-md5.mjs`.

## Applied 2026-06-10 (draw-ledger reversal on void/cancel — finding A3)

Draw-ledger reversal to close the bookkeeping gap: voiding or cancelling a draw order previously consumed the booking balance permanently (no decrement of `quote_product_draws`). Now `void_order` and `cancel_order` both reverse the ledger — full quantity for void, undelivered-only for cancel. Adds `orders.booking_draw boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false` to distinguish draw orders from whole-conversion orders; `draw_down_quote` marks new draw orders. If the parent quote was fully drawn (accepted) and the reversal restores balance, quote reopens to `sent`. F7 hold-deactivation in `cancel_order` skips draw orders (the undrawn booking's holds must survive). 2 reviewers clean (0 BLOCKER/0 HIGH); live census confirmed 0 draw orders (backfill touches 0 rows); self-verify block asserts all invariants at apply time. Disk renamed to MCP stamp per B7.

REVOKE anon/PUBLIC on all 3 fns; self-verify block asserts column existence, overload=1, sentinel strings, grants. |

Rolled-back 9-path e2e smoke ALL PASS — including the exact corrupt state the BLOCKER produced (override-forced `accepted` + partial draws → convert now raises `BOOKING_PARTIALLY_DRAWN` instead of returning `already_converted`), the UI pre-flip simulation (direct `accepted` UPDATE on a partially-drawn quote → blocked by the new trigger), duplicate-key draw → same order returned/no double-draw, final draw → `accepted` allowed, control quote converts normally, no-auth/forged-actor probes correct.

| Version | File | Description |
|---------|------|-------------|
| 20260610181612 | `convert_partially_drawn_guard_first` | **BLOCKER:** QuoteBuilder pre-flips status to `accepted` (releasing all holds) before calling convert, which routed partially-drawn bookings into the `already_converted` short-circuit — silently destroying the undrawn balance. Fix: draws guard hoisted FIRST and made status-independent (partial → `BOOKING_PARTIALLY_DRAWN`; fully drawn → `already_converted`, never re-book); NEW integrity trigger `enforce_quote_accepted_fully_drawn` (BEFORE UPDATE OF status, `_is_admin_override()` hatch) blocks ANY writer from accepting a partially-drawn booking. Frontend: executeConvertToOrder checks the draw ledger before the destructive pre-accept (fail-closed) + `hasRpcCode` mappings for `BOOKING_PARTIALLY_DRAWN`/`BOOKING_CLOSED`. |
| 20260610181726 | `draw_down_idempotency_after_lock` | **HIGH (double-draw TOCTOU):** `check_idempotency` ran before the quotes `FOR UPDATE` lock and the check/save pair is non-atomic — two same-key concurrent requests (double-click/retry) could both pass and double-draw the booking + double-insert commissions. Fix: idempotency check relocated AFTER the lock (still before the status guard so final-draw retries return the cached result, not `BOOKING_CLOSED`); the lock now serializes same-key duplicates. Body otherwise verbatim from live. |

Supports the durable write-ahead-log pattern in `send-email` Edge Function v11: insert pending row BEFORE Resend call, update to sent/failed after. File: `20260813040000_clamp_negative_commission_remainder.sql`, branch `claude/wave-a-money`. Wave A fix #3 of the 2026-08-09 ordering-cycle review. Three functions — `_insert_commissions_for_order`, `_insert_commissions_for_job`, and `_save_invoice_scoped_impl` — give the **last** commission-split row the rounding remainder as `GREATEST(ROUND(profit,2),0) - SUM(earlier rows)`. The `GREATEST` clamps the *total*, not the difference, so the remainder itself can go negative: on a valid four-way 25% split of a $0.02 profit the earlier rows round to 0.01 each, sum to 0.03, and the last row lands at -0.01. `commissions.chk_commission_amount CHECK (commission_amount >= 0)` then aborts the whole transaction with a raw check-constraint error, taking down the entire quote conversion / order creation / invoice save. The fix clamps the last row at zero and caps every earlier row at the budget still unspent, so the rows can never sum past the rounded total. The cap is **inert on every split that succeeds today** — if the old remainder was already >= 0, every running total was within budget and `LEAST()` returns the unchanged per-row share. Measured read-only against live across 15 split shapes: exactly the two currently-aborting shapes change, the other 13 are byte-identical, and every case sums exactly to `GREATEST(ROUND(profit,2),0)` with no negative row. Each `CREATE OR REPLACE` is the exact live statement text (md5-verified against `pg_proc.prosrc`) with only the reconciliation `CASE` rewritten. Pre/postconditions were executed against live read-only on 2026-08-10 and both pass: the precondition ran to its final assertion (all three md5 pins, the `compute_commission_amount` non-negativity clamp across every overload, `_save_invoice_scoped_impl` still `SECURITY DEFINER`, `chk_commission_amount` present), and the postcondition's structural half proved non-vacuous — as-is it fails on the missing clamp marker, softened it passes the overload count, all three `prosecdef` flags, the pinned `search_path`, and the anon/authenticated/PUBLIC EXECUTE-grant check. Catalog lookups are by function **name**, not by a `::regprocedure` signature literal, because a signature literal for a re-declared function aborts with a raw cast error before any readable message can fire; uniqueness is asserted separately. **Not applied, not reviewed by Codex, and blocked behind PR #371.** |

File: `20260813050000_guard_job_commission_split_immutable.sql`, branch `claude/wave-a-money`. Wave A fix #4 of the 2026-08-09 ordering-cycle review. `jobs.commission_split` is the jsonb column read at invoicing time to mint commission rows, and today any signed-in sales rep can rewrite it directly. `jobs_update` is `USING (is_admin() OR is_sales_rep())` with no ownership scoping — unlike `quotes_update`, which *is* scoped for reps — the ACL baseline grants table-wide UPDATE on `public.jobs` to `authenticated`, and `_enforce_billed_job_immutability` enumerates 36 columns of which `commission_split` is not one. A rep can therefore re-point a colleague's commission at themselves through the ordinary REST update path, and the money follows at invoicing. Voiding an invoice returns the job to `completed` and re-invoicing re-mints from the column, so a split rewritten on an invoiced job is not inert. This adds `_guard_job_commission_split_immutable()` (SECURITY INVOKER, pinned `search_path`, EXECUTE revoked from PUBLIC/anon/authenticated/service_role) on a `BEFORE UPDATE OF commission_split` trigger. **Four allowances, in order:** an unchanged rewrite (`IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`) returns immediately; filling a NULL is allowed **only when `current_user` is the owner of `public.jobs`**; a rewrite is allowed while the transaction-local GUC `crx.job_split_correction_authorized` holds **this row's own id**, which only the admin correction RPC described below can set; every other change raises `JOB_COMMISSION_SPLIT_IMMUTABLE`. **The caller check is an allowlist, deliberately** — an earlier draft named the three Supabase API roles and refused them, which fails open for any role nobody thought to list (a future custom role, a Studio SQL-editor session, `dashboard_user`); the shipped form looks the owner up from `pg_class`/`pg_roles` at fire time and refuses everything else. Without a caller check at all, the NULL branch is the original hole restricted to not-yet-invoiced rows, and this guard would then freeze the forgery permanently. Both legitimate writers are `SECURITY DEFINER` owned by the `jobs` table owner (verified live 2026-08-11 **and asserted in the precondition**, because `CREATE OR REPLACE` silently resets a function to SECURITY INVOKER when the clause is omitted and `transfer_job_to_invoice` has been re-emitted several times), so `current_user` is that owner inside them while a REST update runs as an API role; `current_user` is not client-settable, so this is caller identity, not a bypass flag. **Which jobs actually carry a value — corrected from the first draft.** A NULL split is not a rare legacy leftover: `jobs_snapshot_commission_split` fills the column on INSERT only when `quote_id IS NULL`, so every quote-derived job — the primary scheduling path — is inserted NULL and stays NULL until invoicing. The freeze therefore bites at invoicing for those jobs, and the value it freezes comes from the parent quote's split or the customer default, which makes the real control surface there the ownership scoping on `save_quote`/`save_customer`; this guard makes an upstream mistake permanent rather than preventing it. **Trigger order is load-bearing.** Same-timing triggers fire alphabetically by `tgname` (type `name`, C collation), and `trg_guard_…` sorts ahead of `trg_stamp_commission_split_recipient_ids`, so the guard sees the caller's raw NEW rather than the stamper's name→id enrichment. **That ordering is now proved from the catalog, not from a literal.** The first draft compared two string constants, which is a tautology that cannot fail; the shipped precondition queries `pg_trigger`/`pg_proc` for every BEFORE-ROW-UPDATE trigger on `public.jobs` whose function assigns `NEW.commission_split` — matching **both** `NEW.commission_split :=` and `… INTO NEW.commission_split`, since `jobs_snapshot_commission_split` uses both forms — and aborts unless each one sorts strictly after the guard. **Other assertions added after review:** the migration must be applied by the `jobs` table owner (the probe's owner-fill would otherwise abort on a false alarm); `_guard_recipient_name_reuse` must be installed and not disabled, because the unchanged-rewrite allowance delegates to the stamper and is only safe while that guard forbids acquiring a referenced profile name; `save_job` must not assign the column, so ordinary job saves never reach this guard; no `public` function may use a SQL-standard (`BEGIN ATOMIC`) body, which lives in `prosqlbody` and is invisible to every `prosrc` regex in the file; and the writer-detection regex is anchored on the `SET` clause (`UPDATE … SET … commission_split =`, tolerating `UPDATE ONLY` and the `%I`/`%s` of dynamic SQL) so a statement that merely reads the column in a `WHERE` clause is not miscounted as a writer. **The one way through is an audited admin correction (Mason's decision, 2026-08-11).** The first draft exposed no escape hatch at all, which meant a wrong split could only be fixed by writing a migration; Mason chose "let admins correct it, with a record" instead. This migration therefore also creates `public.correct_job_commission_split(p_job_id uuid, p_new_split jsonb, p_reason text, p_performed_by uuid DEFAULT NULL, p_idempotency_key text DEFAULT NULL)` — `SECURITY DEFINER`, pinned `search_path`, EXECUTE revoked from PUBLIC/anon/service_role and granted to `authenticated` only. It requires `auth.uid()`, refuses an `p_performed_by` that disagrees with it, requires `is_admin()`, requires a non-blank reason, revalidates the new value through the existing `validate_commission_split_json`, takes `FOR UPDATE` on the job, returns early and unchanged when the value already matches, and writes a `financial_audit_log` row (`operation_type = 'split_modified'`, `entity_type = 'split'`) recording the old and new values plus the reason. **Three properties make the handshake honest rather than a bypass flag.** The GUC carries the **job id**, not a boolean, so a value left set for one job cannot authorize an edit to a different one in the same transaction; `set_config(..., true)` is transaction-local and is additionally cleared immediately after the UPDATE; and it is only settable from inside an admin-gated `SECURITY DEFINER` function, since a raw PostgREST row update cannot issue `SET LOCAL` at all. The guard trigger **stays `SECURITY INVOKER`** — making it DEFINER would set `current_user` to the table owner and silently void the NULL-fill caller check — and the postcondition asserts `NOT prosecdef` on it. `SECURITY DEFINER` on the RPC is not a preference: `financial_audit_log` grants INSERT to `postgres` only, so a caller-rights function physically could not write its own audit row. The audit row records the value read back with `RETURNING`, not the value requested, because the stamper enriches recipient ids after the guard runs. **The bulk-repair path is unchanged and still available:** `ALTER TABLE public.jobs DISABLE TRIGGER …` / `ENABLE TRIGGER` inside a reviewed migration — owner-only, unreachable from any Supabase API role, and visible in the diff. Precedent: migration `20260722174029_commission_split_recipient_ids` carried a top-level backfill that this guard would have refused. **What changes for the office:** nobody loses the ability to fix a mistake; they lose the ability to fix one invisibly. A rep can no longer rewrite a split at all, and an admin can, but every correction leaves a dated row naming who changed it, from what, to what, and why. This brings the guard in line with its sibling `_enforce_billed_job_immutability`, which already exempts admins so they can correct billed history. **Live evidence 2026-08-11 (read-only).** The precondition — including all four new assertions — was executed against production byte-identically to the migration's own copy and ran to `PRECOND_VALIDATION_ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED`: applier is the table owner, single jsonb column, stamper present, no competing assigning trigger sorts ahead of the guard, `_guard_recipient_name_reuse` live on `profiles` and enabled, `save_job` clean, no SQL-standard bodies anywhere in `public`, the hardened regex still returns exactly two writers (`transfer_job_to_invoice`, `_save_field_app_split_invoice_impl`) both writing through the fill-only `COALESCE(commission_split, …)` pattern, and both `prosecdef` and owned by the `jobs` owner. **The correction path's own preconditions were then verified live, read-only, on 2026-08-11:** all four borrowed dependencies exist (`validate_commission_split_json`, `is_admin`, `check_idempotency`, `save_idempotency`); `financial_audit_log_operation_type_check` already permits `'split_modified'` and `financial_audit_log_entity_type_check` already permits `'split'`, so **no CHECK-constraint widening is needed** and this migration adds none; and production currently has 4 active admins, 1 active sales rep, 3 jobs with a split set and 1 with a NULL split — every row and role shape the probes require, so none of them will fall back to a weaker proof. **One real bug was caught here before it shipped:** `check_idempotency` returns NULL on a NULL key but `save_idempotency` *raises* `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED` on one, so both save calls are wrapped in `IF p_idempotency_key IS NOT NULL`, matching the `complete_team_note` precedent. Without that, every correction made without an idempotency key would have failed **after** rewriting the split. **A probe from the first draft was removed as provably wrong.** It fired an API-role no-op save to prove the REVOKE had not broken browser writes, on the rationale that a trigger fire might be privilege-checked. PostgreSQL checks EXECUTE on a trigger function at `CREATE TRIGGER` time, not each time it fires, so the probe tested nothing; the same conclusion is independently supported by 40 existing production triggers that already have EXECUTE revoked from `authenticated` on tables the browser writes daily, and by the trigger being scoped `UPDATE OF commission_split` on a column `save_job` never writes. **The behavioural probe is exercised at apply time and rolls itself back.** It hard-fails rather than skipping if either row shape is missing, and live currently has both. It proves seven things: an owner rewrite of a set split is refused; a no-op rewrite is allowed; an API-role fill of a NULL is refused, which is the caller check itself; an owner-level fill of a NULL still succeeds, which is the invoicing path; **the GUC is job-scoped, proved by setting it to a different job's id and confirming the rewrite is still refused** — the single most important assertion in the file, because if that ever starts passing the correction path has degraded into a global switch; a non-admin calling the correction RPC is refused with `ADMIN_REQUIRED`, exercised under a real active sales rep's identity via a transaction-local `request.jwt.claims`; and a real active admin's correction succeeds, returns `changed = true`, and leaves **exactly one** new `financial_audit_log` row, with the GUC verified empty on return. That last one hard-fails rather than skipping if live has no active admin: do not install this guard without watching an admin correction actually succeed. Both new probes disclose in the header that they call the RPC for real — one split rewritten, one audit row inserted — and both are rolled back with the rest of the probe block. The role-switching probe captures `current_user` up front and restores it with `SET LOCAL ROLE %I` rather than `RESET ROLE`, which would drop to the session login role and run the owner-only probe under the wrong identity, and it asserts the restore actually took effect before that probe runs. The no-op probe re-fires the stamper, so a fail-closed recipient-resolution error is re-raised with a message naming the row and the stamper instead of surfacing as an unexplained guard failure. Residue is proven by hashing every split on the table in id order before and after and requiring the hashes to match — the sentinel-string check it replaced was vacuous, since the sentinel only ever appears in writes the guard refuses. The overload check is documented as a tripwire rather than a proof: a zero-argument signature cannot be overloaded under `CREATE OR REPLACE`, so it exists to catch a future edit that adds a parameter. **Not applied, not reviewed by Codex, and blocked behind PR #371.** |

File: `20260813060000_require_completed_delivery_before_invoice_post.sql`, branch `claude/wave-a-money`. Wave A fix #5 of the 2026-08-09 ordering-cycle review, shape chosen by Mason on 2026-08-11: **an invoice tied to a delivery cannot be posted until that delivery is actually completed.** Today it can. `_create_quick_delivery_intent_impl_20260802` inserts the delivery row with `status = 'scheduled'` and, in the same call, creates the draft invoice carrying that `delivery_id` — so a bill exists for goods still in the warehouse, and posting it succeeds. **Why that is a money bug, not a policy preference.** The draft is created at *ordered* quantity. `_complete_delivery_authorized_impl`'s adjustment loop only rewrites invoices whose status is still `'draft'`, so posting first makes the delivery-time correction skip the invoice and freezes the customer at the ordered quantity even when less was delivered. `trg_snapshot_line_shares_on_post` also freezes line shares at post time, which is why widening the adjustment loop to posted invoices is the wrong repair — gating the post is the right one. **One function covers all three posting paths.** `_post_invoice_impl_20260714(p_invoice_id uuid, p_idempotency_key text DEFAULT NULL)` is the only function that flips `invoices.status` to `'posted'` on a normal path; exactly two functions reference it (`_post_invoice_customer_scope_impl`, `_post_invoice_group_customer_scope_impl`) and every user-facing entry point funnels through those — `post_invoice` → `_post_invoice_idem_impl_20260721` → `_post_invoice_public_impl_20260718` → customer-scope → impl; `post_invoice_group` → group-customer-scope → impl; `batch_post_invoices` loops `post_invoice`. One `CREATE OR REPLACE` therefore closes all three, and the precondition asserts that caller set by name so a fourth path cannot appear unnoticed. The single writer that sets `'posted'` itself, `_post_deleted_delivery_recovery_invoice_20260719`, already requires `d.status = 'completed'`; the precondition asserts that too, and separately asserts that **no other** function writes `invoices.status = 'posted'`. **The gate.** When `invoices.delivery_id IS NOT NULL`, the delivery row is read and the post is refused with `DELIVERY_MISSING` if the row is gone, or `DELIVERY_NOT_COMPLETED` if it is soft-deleted or its status is anything other than `'completed'`. The refusal text names the delivery and tells the office what to do — complete the delivery, which is the same step that corrects the invoice to the quantities actually delivered, or void the draft if the delivery was cancelled or voided. **The delivery row is read without a lock, deliberately.** `_complete_delivery_authorized_impl` locks the delivery *before* the invoice, and the posting impl already holds `FOR UPDATE` on the invoice; taking a delivery lock inside the gate would reverse that order and deadlock. The residual window is stated honestly rather than talked around, and it is **not** one-directional: if a delivery is voided or soft-deleted in the instant between the unlocked read and the invoice UPDATE, the post proceeds even though the gate would have refused it a moment later. That is the same outcome as today's un-gated behaviour and is not made worse by this file, and `void_delivery` already has its own handling for a delivery whose invoice is already posted. Closing the window properly means reordering the locks inside `_complete_delivery_authorized_impl`, which is a separate change with its own deadlock analysis. **What is deliberately not gated, and why.** Job, application and standalone invoices carry no `delivery_id` and are untouched. Order-level invoices created by `_create_invoice_from_order_impl_20260718` also carry no `delivery_id`, and that function already **refuses to run** when the order has any delivery not in ('cancelled','voided') — it is the deliberate "cancel the deliveries and bill the whole order by hand" escape, and live currently holds 0 invoices of that shape. Gating those on `orders.status = 'fulfilled'` was considered and rejected from live evidence: every writer of that column is delivery-driven, so an order with no deliveries can never reach `'fulfilled'` and such invoices would become permanently unpostable. Credit memos and finance charges are unaffected. **Fails closed on drift.** Because `CREATE OR REPLACE` rewrites the whole body, the precondition pins the live body to md5 `9479af0a5477e89266e0264da44c766c` — the exact text read from production on 2026-08-11 — and **every** other arm aborts: an unrecognised hash aborts telling the applier to re-derive from current live source, and — deliberately — so does the already-installed case, because a second apply would overwrite whatever the live body has become since with the copy frozen on 2026-08-11. A sibling session's fix cannot be silently reverted by this file. **Atomicity is explicit.** The whole file runs inside one top-level `BEGIN;`/`COMMIT;`, the shape 30 already-applied migrations in this repo use. Without it, a non-transactional applier could leave the gate switched on in production while the probe below reported failure; with it, any raise anywhere reverts the function to exactly what it was. **What changes for the office: nothing breaks.** All delivery-linked invoices on live today already point at completed deliveries, so no existing draft becomes unpostable; the precondition also raises a notice counting any draft the gate would hold, so the applier sees the real number at apply time rather than trusting this sentence. **The behavioural probe runs at apply time and rolls itself back.** Its authoritative rollback evidence is **row-level**: the one invoice row and the one delivery row the probe writes are hashed whole with `md5(to_jsonb(row)::text)` before and after, and a mismatch aborts. A whole-table fingerprint of `invoices` and `deliveries` also runs but was **downgraded to a `RAISE NOTICE` after review** — under READ COMMITTED every statement takes a fresh snapshot, so an ordinary office edit committed by another session mid-apply would move a whole-table fingerprint through no fault of the probe, and aborting a money migration with "the rollback did not hold" when it did hold is the worst message this file could produce. The row hashes cover every column rather than a hand-picked list, so a future status-change trigger stamping `cancelled_at`, `last_edited_by` or similar cannot slip past; they are hashed rather than compared as text so an abort message can never print a live invoice row into a public PR. Everything else a real post writes (`financial_audit_log`, `activity_feed`, `rup_sales_records`, `notifications`, `invoice_line_share_snapshots`) is covered by the subtransaction rollback itself, which unwinds every table equally; the only genuinely irreversible cost is any sequence value consumed, which is cosmetic. Under a real active admin's forged `request.jwt.claims`, and bracketing each delivery-status UPDATE with a transaction-local `app.admin_override` that is **cleared again before every post attempt** so the gate is always exercised without it — the live transition trigger allows only scheduled→in_progress/cancelled and in_progress→completed/cancelled, so without that override the probe could not move the row at all and an earlier draft of this file could never have applied — it (a) flips a postable delivery-linked draft's delivery to `scheduled` — the exact quick-delivery shape this file exists to stop — and then to `cancelled`, requiring `DELIVERY_NOT_COMPLETED` each time, (b) soft-deletes the delivery while leaving its status `'completed'` and requires refusal — proving the deleted-check is not shadowed by the status check — and (c) restores the delivery and **posts for real**, requiring the invoice to reach `'posted'`, so the allow path is proved and not merely the deny path. That allow arm surfaces `SQLERRM` in its failure message so an unrelated cause, such as a closed accounting period, is not misread as the gate. **The ACL is made active, not merely asserted.** `REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION public._post_invoice_impl_20260714(uuid, text) FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated, service_role` runs after the `CREATE OR REPLACE` (which preserves existing grants). The live ACL read `postgres=X/postgres` on 2026-08-11, so this is a no-op today; it is here because this is the *inner* implementation — the customer-scope and idempotency-payload-binding checks live in its two SECURITY DEFINER callers — so any client role holding EXECUTE here would skip those as well as reaching this gate. The postcondition then asserts no client role holds EXECUTE, closing the B7/B8/B9 shape by construction rather than by inspection. **Catalog lookups avoid `pg_get_function_identity_arguments()`.** The LIVE-DATA GUARD denies that builtin as "not a known read-only function", which would make this block impossible to rehearse read-only before applying (the guard runs on the ad-hoc SQL path only, so it would not have blocked the apply itself — but losing the dry-run on a money file is not a trade worth making); the signature assertion is written as plain catalog column reads (`p.pronargs = 2 AND p.proargtypes[0] = 'uuid'::regtype AND p.proargtypes[1] = 'text'::regtype`), which is exactly equivalent and calls nothing. **Second review round (2026-08-11), both reviewers, 0 BLOCKERs.** Both independently found the same real defect and it is fixed: the completeness assertions counted the definitions that *matched* a guard and required the count to be 1, which passes in exactly the case they exist to catch — add a second, unguarded overload beside a guarded one and the count is unchanged. PRECOND F, G and P are now inverted to **count the definitions that FAIL the guard and require zero**, each paired with a new existence assertion (F2, G2, P2) so that deleting the function outright cannot satisfy a zero-failures test vacuously. Also from that round: PRECOND B widened to pin the return type, parameter names and the trailing DEFAULT (all three are things `CREATE OR REPLACE` refuses to change, and it would otherwise abort with a bare PostgreSQL message that says nothing about billing); PRECOND I gained `DISTINCT`; a **new PRECOND Q** pins the `trg_invoice_draft_insert` / `enforce_invoice_draft_on_insert` backstop as present, enabled and BEFORE INSERT ROW; `statement_timeout` raised 60s → 180s because the postcondition block is one statement covering four real post attempts and every trigger they fire; the EXECUTE assertion extended to `metabase_ro` behind a `pg_roles` existence guard; the probe's error matching narrowed from `LIKE 'DELIVERY_NOT_COMPLETED%'` (underscores are single-character wildcards in a LIKE pattern) to `position(...) = 1`, and **`DELIVERY_MISSING` is no longer accepted there** — the probe only UPDATEs the delivery status and never removes the row, so accepting it would let a genuinely broken state read as the gate working; a `COALESCE(o.deleted_at,'epoch')` comparison replaced by plain `IS NULL`; and a dead `current_user`-unchanged assertion deleted outright rather than left as decoration. The block went from 14 assertions to 20. **The full 20-assertion block was then dry-run read-only against production on 2026-08-11 and every assertion passed**, with the blocked-draft count coming back **zero** — no invoice that exists today becomes unpostable. That dry-run needed one wording change to run at all, and the cause is worth recording because it is not obvious: PRECOND I's *English error message* read "the set of functions that INSERT into invoices…", and the LIVE-DATA GUARD matches statement text rather than effect, so it read that prose as a real write against the live `invoices` table and refused the entire read-only statement. Reworded to "add new rows to invoices" — the same class of false positive as the earlier `snapshot(s)` case, and the same fix (reword, never bypass). The guard was also read directly to settle the related worry: `live-testdata-guard.mjs:21` returns early unless the tool name matches `execute_sql`, so it never sees `apply_migration`. Guard-tripping prose in a migration therefore costs the rehearsal, not the apply. **Third review round (2026-08-11), both reviewers again, 0 BLOCKERs; the block is now 21 assertions.** Four HIGH findings, two of which turned on facts only production could settle, so both were probed read-only before anything was changed. (1) *The `prosrc` blind spot.* Every completeness scan in this block searches `pg_proc.prosrc`, the stored text of a function's body. PostgreSQL 14 added a second way to write one (`LANGUAGE sql … BEGIN ATOMIC`) whose body is **not** kept there, so such a function would be invisible to the very scans that exist to prove nothing else posts an invoice. The reviewer's specific mechanism — that `NOT (prosrc ~* …)` would swallow those rows as NULL — is **wrong on this database**: a live probe on PostgreSQL 17.6 found 56 such functions, **all with a blank-string `prosrc`, none NULL**, so the inverted assertions F, G and P fail closed as intended. The underlying worry was still real for the *set*-shaped assertions E, H and I, which would simply not see such a function at all. Fixed by a **new PRECOND R** asserting that **zero** functions in the `public` schema use a SQL-standard body — true today, all 56 live in extension schemas — so if that ever changes the apply stops and says the scans must be re-derived rather than quietly trusting them. (2) *PRECOND Q was too loose.* It confirmed the `trg_invoice_draft_insert` backstop exists and is enabled but not **when** it fires, so an `INSTEAD OF` or `AFTER` trigger of the same name would have satisfied it. Now pinned with `(t.tgtype & 71) = 7`, which in one test requires FOR EACH ROW + BEFORE + INSERT and excludes INSTEAD OF — the live value is exactly 7 — plus `tgenabled IN ('O','A')`. (3) *The blocked-draft count was structurally blind.* It used an inner join from `invoices` to `deliveries`, which **drops** exactly the rows where the delivery is missing — the new `DELIVERY_MISSING` class the count exists to measure. Live evidence says that class is currently unreachable (`invoices_delivery_id_fkey` is a **VALIDATED** foreign key with **0** dangling references), but the FK is not something this block asserts, so the count should not silently depend on it: switched to a LEFT JOIN. (4) *The filename re-stamp*, which is an apply-time obligation already written into the file's header and repeated below. Also folded in that round: the gate's status test changed from `<>` to `IS DISTINCT FROM`, because `<>` against a NULL yields NULL, the `IF` never fires and the post proceeds — the wrong direction for a money gate to fail if that column's nullability ever changes; the four role-privilege checks in the postcondition collapsed into a single `EXISTS` over `pg_roles`, because `has_function_privilege` **errors** on a role that does not exist rather than returning false, which had made this file unappliable against any database missing `anon`, `authenticated` or `service_role` (a container replay harness is exactly that shape), with the `metabase_ro` revoke wrapped in the same existence guard; the external-effect sweep extended to name the Supabase Database Webhook path (`supabase_functions.http_request`), `pg_net` (`net.http_get` / `net.http_post`) and `pg_notify` — all of them unwound by the subtransaction or deferred to top-level commit anyway, but the enumeration is what this file offers as evidence, so the enumeration had to be complete; a wrong `lock_timeout` comment corrected, since it bounds how long this transaction **waits** for a lock and not how long the probe **holds** one (locks are held until COMMIT either way); and the header's "the refusal reaches the client" claim scoped away from `batch_post_invoices`, which catches per-invoice errors and returns them as a `failures` array rather than raising, so `describePostInvoiceBlock` in `src/lib/db.ts` — which only inspects a thrown error — does not translate them there. All prior scenarios re-run clean against this body. **A third adversarial pass found one more HIGH, CRX-MONEY-001, closed by an apply-time guard, and a fourth pass then widened that guard.** The new body takes any already-billed line matching no price tier off the FRONT of the tier list. Such a line can only come from a draw made before this migration, when the old code billed one quantity-weighted average. Front-of-list conserves quantity but not money: the average consumed the tiers proportionally, so retiring the cheapest units first leaves the dearer tiers to bill and the booking bills out above its own value — a 100-at-$1.00 plus 100-at-$2.00 booking, partially drawn at the $1.50 average, would bill $325.00 against a $300.00 booking, and `DRAW_ALLOCATION_MISMATCH` would not catch it because it proves quantity was allocated, not that the right monetary tiers were consumed. The first guard tested whether a billed line matched no tier, and the fourth adversarial pass showed that test is too narrow: a weighted average can land exactly on a real tier — 100 each at $1.00, $2.00 and $3.00 averages to $2.00 — and then the tier-matching join subtracts the whole legacy quantity from a tier that cannot hold it, the clamp discards the excess, and the booking bills out *below* its value. The test that would catch the first case passes precisely when the second one happens. The guard is therefore no longer a price test at all: it refuses to apply if any still-drawable booking carries more than one price tier for a product **and** that pair was already drawn under the weighted-average code, whatever it was billed at, because the average does not carry the information needed to recover which tiers those units consumed. Evidence of a prior draw is read from either side — a surviving booking-draw order line or a `quote_product_draws` ledger row — so a voided order still counts. The tier key is the `(price_per_unit, cost_at_quote_cents)` pair, so two lines at the same price with different snapshot costs are two tiers. It refuses with `DRAW_DOWN_PREMIGRATION_MIXED_TIER_DRAW`. Inferring the historical allocation was considered and deliberately rejected, as was a proportional skip: the first would write a guess into customer money, and the second would add new integer-allocation math to a path that holds zero rows now and can hold none after apply, since every draw from here on writes tier-keyed lines that match. Measured read-only against live on 2026-08-15 and again on 2026-08-16, no quote carries more than one price tier for the same product, so nothing is affected today — but a measurement is not an apply-time guarantee, and the current live code still accepts a mixed-price booking whenever its average lands on a whole cent, so one could be created and partially drawn between review and apply. Proven in both directions on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.14 database with the guard text extracted verbatim from the migration, across seven scenarios: it raised and counted exactly 4 — the average matching no tier, the average landing on a real tier, the coincidence case recorded only in the draw ledger behind a voided order, and two lines at one price with differing costs — while three controls contributed nothing, namely a single-tier booking drawn at an odd price, a soft-deleted mixed-tier booking, and, most importantly, an ordinary mixed-tier booking with no draw yet, which is exactly the case this migration exists to serve and which the guard must never block. With only the four hazards’ draw evidence removed and all three controls intact, the same block completed silently. **A fourth adversarial pass found one more HIGH, CRX-MONEY-002, and it is closed in two halves.** `quote_items.total_units_needed` is `numeric` with no CHECK, so a negative or non-finite booked quantity is representable. The per-product balance sums every one of the product’s quote lines, negatives included, while the tier pool takes only lines above zero — the averaging code this replaces read one weighted price over the same negative-inclusive set, so a negative line pulled the billed price down, and the split cannot do that because a negative line has no tier to be billed at. A booking of 100 units at $2.00 and −50 units at $4.00 is worth $0.00 and still reports 50 units drawable: the old code billed those 50 at the $0.00 average, the split would take all 50 from the $2.00 tier and invoice $100.00 against a booking worth nothing. The conservation assertion cannot catch it, because excluding the negative line makes the tier pool larger than the balance, never smaller, and that assertion fires only when the pool is too small. The function body now refuses such a draw with `BOOKING_QUANTITY_INVALID` before writing anything, and the migration additionally adds a validated CHECK, `quote_items_total_units_needed_nonneg_finite_chk`, so the value cannot be written at all; the body still refuses rather than trusting the constraint, because a constraint can be dropped and this path prices customer money. The finiteness half is not decoration: PostgreSQL orders NaN above every number, so a sign test alone would admit NaN. Verified read-only against production on 2026-08-16 that the column carries no CHECK today and that no row holds a negative or non-finite quantity, so the constraint is added validated rather than NOT VALID, and no existing row is rejected by it. Postflight asserts the constraint is present, validated, and carries both halves of its definition. Proven on fresh throwaway PostgreSQL 16.14 databases: the constraint rejects −1, NaN, Infinity and −Infinity by name while accepting NULL, zero and a positive quantity; the function body, on a database with the constraint deliberately absent, refuses the exploit booking and writes no order and no draw-ledger row, while the same booking with the second line made positive still draws all 150 units and bills exactly $400.00 as two tier lines. Mutation-checked against the pre-fix body on the identical fixture, which drew the exploit booking and billed $100.00 against a booking worth $0.00. Under constraint-name drift that pair is not enough: a same-named weaker rule can contain both tokens and still admit the values the constraint exists to stop. Proven on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.14 database — a same-named rule joining the two halves with OR instead of AND stored −1 successfully, and the old substring postflight passed it. Both halves now compare the stored rule to the exact expression PostgreSQL normalises this CHECK to, captured from `pg_get_constraintdef` rather than hand-written: if the name is already taken by a different rule the migration aborts with `CONSTRAINT_NAME_DRIFT` instead of adopting it unread, and the postflight asserts equality rather than substring presence. Re-proven end to end on fresh throwaway databases: on a clean database the block creates the constraint, the postflight passes, and the constraint rejects −1, NaN, Infinity and −Infinity by name while accepting NULL and a positive quantity; on a database carrying the weaker same-named rule the block aborts. **The same pass raised CRX-MIG-001, a high, and it was a stale branch base rather than an edit:** this branch had never touched `.claude/schema-registry.json`, but it was cut before #406 refreshed that file from live introspection, so merging would have rolled the registry back a day and dropped an applied security migration from its list. Both gate reviewers must be re-run against this text before any live apply, and the schema registry must be refreshed after apply because this migration now adds a constraint as well as replacing a function. **A sixth adversarial pass found one more HIGH, and it is closed in two halves.** The mixed-tier apply-time guard above scanned only bookings in `sent` or `revised` status — the two statuses a draw is allowed from — on the reasoning that a booking which cannot be drawn today cannot be mispriced by this path. That reasoning is wrong, because “drawable” is not a stable property of a booking. Drawing one to completion flips it to `accepted`, and every void/cancel reversal path flips `accepted` back to `sent` as soon as a partial cancel, cancel or void leaves it no longer fully drawn (`20260610185806`, `20260613191323`, `20260616142001`, `20260620130000`, `20260721014858`). A booking drawn to completion under the averaging code would therefore have passed the guard, reopened later, and had its remainder allocated with no record of which tiers the average consumed — the same misbill as before, just deferred: 100 units at $1.00 plus 100 at $2.00 drawn at the $1.50 average, then 50 delivered and the remainder cancelled, bills $325.00 against a $300.00 booking, and quantity still conserves so `DRAW_ALLOCATION_MISMATCH` stays silent. The status filter is therefore removed: the guard now keys on the stable predicate — this product on this booking carries more than one tier **and** already carries draw evidence — accepting that a genuinely finished booking will be refused too, a false refusal a human clears once, which is the fail-closed direction and the correct trade against writing a guess into customer money. Proven on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.14 database by running both scan texts against one fixture: the old scan refused only the `sent` booking and let the `accepted` one through exactly as reported, the new scan refuses both, and neither refuses either control — a single-tier drawn booking and a mixed-tier booking with no draw. The same pass also found the cutover unserialised: the scan took no lock against the old draw body, so a draw that started before the scan could commit after it and be missed, defeating the apply-time guarantee. The migration now takes `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` on `quote_product_draws` — the table every draw path writes — before the preflight, held for the applier’s single transaction, so a concurrent legacy draw either commits before the lock and is seen by the scan or blocks and resumes against the new body. Proven on the same database: while that lock is held a concurrent INSERT and a concurrent UPDATE both fail with `canceling statement due to lock timeout`, a plain SELECT is unaffected, and a draw succeeds again once the lock is released. The top-level lock form is confirmed legal for this applier by three migrations already applied live that use it (`20260702135000`, `20260716233000`, `20260717101619`), and the amended file was run in a single transaction to confirm the lock executes and the preflight is reached. That is sound for lines the old averaging code wrote, but not for a line whose key was rewritten after it was billed — the tier it was really drawn from stays in the pool, and both get sold. (3) *The cutover lock cannot drain a draw that is already running.* `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` blocks an old invocation only when it reaches its ledger write, and that invocation keeps executing the old function body out of its own plan cache after the replacement commits, with its uncommitted rows invisible to the scan. The previous entry’s claim that such a draw “resumes against the new body” was wrong and has been corrected in the file. Eliminating the window needs a barrier inside the OLD body, which can only ship in an earlier, separate migration. What ships here is the net: a late legacy averaged draw leaves exactly the unmatched billed line that guard (1) refuses, so the next draw on that booking stops loudly instead of quietly misbilling the remainder. The window is narrow and no longer silent; it is not closed, and the file no longer claims otherwise. Proven on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.14 database, with both predicates lifted verbatim out of the migration so the test cannot drift from it. Runtime guard: the reported scenario refuses (2 tiers, 50 unmatched units); a single-tier booking with an orphaned line is allowed; a mixed-tier booking mid-partial-draw with every line matching is allowed; a mixed-tier booking with no draw yet — the case this migration exists to serve — is allowed. Both gate reviewers must be re-run against this text before any live apply. **An eighth adversarial pass returned two more HIGHs, both confirmed against real source before any change was made, and both now closed by one guard.** (1) *A coincidental average defeats the seventh pass's unmatched-line net.* That guard refuses a further draw when a billed line matches no price tier, which is the trace a legacy weighted-average draw normally leaves. But an average can land exactly on a real tier key — 100 units each at $1.00, $2.00 and $3.00 averages to $2.00 — and then the line matches, the guard stays silent, and a late legacy draw of 250 units billed at the coincidental $2.00 lets the next 50-unit draw close a $600.00 booking at $550.00. (2) *A supported quote revision silently overconsumes a matching tier.* This one needs no admin hand-edit and no race. `save_quote`'s drawn-product guard (`20260812115236`, read and confirmed rather than assumed) is aggregate-only: it sums draw-ledger rows by `product_id`, sums `quote_items.total_units_needed` by `product_id`, and refuses only when total booked is less than total drawn. It preserves no per-tier attribution. So book 200 units at $2.00, draw 150 of them, then revise the booking to 100 units at $1.00 plus 100 at $2.00. Booked still covers drawn, so the revision saves. The 150 billed units still match the $2.00 tier, which now holds only 100 — and the per-tier `GREATEST(..., 0)` clamp silently discarded that 50-unit overhang, so the $1.00 tier still read as fully available and the remaining 50 units billed against it: $350.00 against a revised $300.00 booking. Neither existing refusal could fire — the balance guard works on per-product aggregates, and `DRAW_ALLOCATION_MISMATCH` fires only when the tier pool is too SMALL, never when it is too large. The previous entry's assertion that the clamp was "bounded on both sides" by those two was therefore false, and the file's own comment saying so has been corrected rather than quietly dropped. Closed with a second runtime layer, `DRAW_TIER_OVERCONSUMED`: the quantity the clamp used to discard is now carried out of the tier query as its own column, accumulated across every tier (the loop no longer exits at the allocation boundary, so tiers past that point are still inspected), and any nonzero total refuses the draw outright. It catches both findings — the coincidental average is attributed wholly to the one tier it happens to match while it really consumed several, so it over-bills that tier and stops here. The durable fix for both remains immutable tier provenance on the order line, which is a schema change deliberately out of scope for this migration; this refusal is the fail-closed stand-in and is deliberately stricter than strictly necessary. Postflight now also asserts both new guard identifiers are present in the shipped body, alongside the existing conservation-assertion tripwire; each of the three was mutation-checked and goes red when its guard is absent. Proven on a throwaway PostgreSQL 17.10 database with the whole tier/billed query lifted verbatim out of the migration so the test cannot drift from it, across seven scenarios: the revised-booking case refuses with zero unmatched units — proving the seventh-pass guard genuinely would not have caught it — the coincidental-average case refuses likewise, and five controls are all still allowed, namely an ordinary partial draw, a fully drawn booking, a single-tier booking with an orphaned legacy line, a booking whose over-billing sits behind a voided order, and one behind a cancelled order with partial delivery. The amended file was then run statement by statement with zero syntax errors and the replacement body compiles with both new guards present in `prosrc`. **A documentation defect was also corrected in this pass:** five earlier entries above described their throwaway proof server as PostgreSQL 17 when it was in fact PostgreSQL 16.14, and they now say so. The two claims in that set that actually depend on the server version were re-proven on a real PostgreSQL 17.10 throwaway: the CHECK constraint normalises to exactly the expression the migration compares against — byte-identical on both 16.14 and 17.10, so the recorded expression was right and only its provenance was misstated — and the constraint still rejects a negative quantity, NaN, Infinity and −Infinity by name while accepting NULL, zero and a positive quantity. Live remains PostgreSQL 17.6. Both gate reviewers must be re-run against this text before any live apply. **A ninth adversarial pass returned one more HIGH, CRX-MONEY-CUTOVER-001, and closing it properly required a second migration, so this one no longer ships alone.** The finding is a smaller variant of the hole the eighth pass closed, and it survives both runtime nets. `DRAW_TIER_OVERCONSUMED` fires only when billed units exceed the tier they match, and `DRAW_MIXED_TIER_UNMATCHED_LINE` fires only when some billed quantity matches no tier at all. Book 100 units each at $1.00, $2.00 and $3.00 with equal cost and the weighted average is exactly $2.00; an in-flight legacy draw of 50 units then writes a 50-unit line at $2.00 that matches the real $2.00 tier and fits comfortably inside its 100-unit capacity. Nothing is unmatched, nothing is overconsumed, both guards stay silent, and those 50 units should have billed at $1.00 — the order, the profit, the commission basis and the audit amount are each wrong by $50.00. The reviewer was right that a runtime net is the wrong instrument here and that the cutover needs a deterministic barrier rather than an operational "apply when no draws are in flight" instruction. **The reviewer's own prescribed remedy was then tested and found unsafe, and the design changed because of the measurement rather than the argument.** The prescription was to have the draw entry point take an advisory lock and let this migration take the same lock exclusively, so draws WAIT. Measured on a throwaway PostgreSQL 17.10 database, that is wrong and silently so: a session whose plan cache already held the pre-cutover implementation, blocking inside a second call for a measured 4.0 seconds spanning the replacement, resumed and still returned the OLD result, because a backend does not re-check plan invalidations in the middle of an already-started command. A waiting barrier would have converted a rare race into a reliable one. What ships instead is a fail-fast barrier in a separate precursor migration, `20260816110000`, recorded in its own row below and applied FIRST. Draws call `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock_shared(20260816, 1)`, which returns immediately: with the key free the draw proceeds exactly as today holding it in SHARE mode, and with the key held exclusively the draw raises `DRAW_DOWN_CUTOVER_IN_PROGRESS` as its very first act and rolls back having written nothing. This migration now takes the same key with `pg_advisory_xact_lock` before its table lock, which yields three exhaustive cases: a draw that took SHARE first holds it to commit, so this migration blocks and the preflight scan sees that draw's rows; a draw arriving while this migration holds the key exclusively is refused and records nothing; and a draw arriving after commit finds the key free and is planned fresh, so it runs the new body. **There is no interval in which the old body can commit a row this scan did not see, so the window the seventh and eighth passes could only narrow is now eliminated, and the file's cutover comment has been rewritten to say so instead of calling it an operational choice.** The lock ordering is advisory-key-then-table on both sides, so no deadlock is possible between a draw and this cutover. The barrier is not merely assumed to be live: the preflight here refuses to run unless the live wrapper actually carries it, asserting the wrapper is the only function of its name, that both the try-lock call and the refusal identifier are present in its body — a lock with no refusal is the broken waiting form — and that the barrier precedes the forwarded implementation call, since a barrier taken after the call is not a barrier. It aborts with `DRAW_DOWN_CUTOVER_BARRIER_MISSING`, `DRAW_DOWN_CUTOVER_BARRIER_MISORDERED` or `DRAW_DOWN_WRAPPER_OVERLOADED`, so the two migrations cannot be applied out of order and this one cannot be applied alone. That is the durable proof gate the reviewer asked for. Proven on a throwaway PostgreSQL 17.10 database rather than argued. The barrier gate here was lifted verbatim out of this file and run against four wrapper variants: it passes only against the correctly barriered wrapper, and refuses a wrapper with no barrier, a wrapper carrying the waiting form with no refusal, a wrapper whose barrier sits after the forwarded call, and a second unbarriered overload. The whole file was then split into its eight statements and each parsed individually with zero syntax errors — the replacement implementation body compiles in full — and the new advisory-lock statement was confirmed to execute. **Both gate reviewers must be re-run against this text, and the pair must be applied in order — `20260816110000` first, then this one — before any live apply.** **Tenth pass (RLS/security + drift review, 2026-08-16).** The security reviewer found that the barrier binds every draw *planned* after the precursor commits but cannot bind a backend already executing the pre-barrier body at that moment: `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` neither interrupts nor drains a running call, so that backend holds no advisory key, and if it has not yet reached its draw-ledger insert the `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` lock finds nothing to conflict with and the preflight scan cannot see its uncommitted rows. The fix is a refusal, not an instruction: the preflight now aborts with `DRAW_DOWN_CUTOVER_NOT_QUIET` if ANY other client-backend transaction older than its own is open — a strict superset of the dangerous set, since this transaction necessarily begins after the precursor commits. Blindness is refused first: a role that cannot read other backends' transaction start times would count zero for the wrong reason, so the gate aborts with `DRAW_DOWN_CUTOVER_STATS_BLIND` unless the applying role is superuser or holds `pg_read_all_stats`. **Operator consequences: the apply needs a genuinely quiet database — expect repeated refusals during business hours — and must run as a role holding `pg_monitor` (confirmed read-only on 2026-08-16 that the applying role does).** `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 15s` now precedes the lock block, so a blocked apply aborts having changed nothing instead of freezing the quote pages; the header no longer claims the migration has no lock footprint, since validating the new CHECK reads every existing row of the quote-items table under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`. The drift review then flagged that bundling both migrations into one transaction would defeat the barrier entirely — it never becomes visible to another session, every concurrent draw runs unbarriered, and the catalog assertions still pass by reading the transaction's own uncommitted catalog — and that only prose forbade it. That is now a guard: the preflight compares `pg_proc.xmin` on the wrapper row against its own transaction id and aborts with `DRAW_DOWN_CUTOVER_BARRIER_UNCOMMITTED`. Proven, not argued, on PostgreSQL 17.10 against a fixture reproducing both live body hashes exactly: applied separately, both migrations succeed with their postflight notices; bundled into one transaction, the apply is refused and rolls back with the wrapper still at its pre-barrier hash. The quiet gate itself was mutation-tested four ways — quiet passes, a concurrent open transaction is refused by name and age, a role without stats visibility is refused, and the same role passes once granted — so it fails closed rather than vacuously. Nine statements now, up from eight. Eleventh pass (RLS/security + drift re-review, 2026-08-16; 0 BLOCKERS from both): the reviewers found no security or schema defect but four *false claims in the header comments*, which on this file are load-bearing because its safety argument is the deliverable. Corrected: `DRAW_TIER_OVERCONSUMED` was described as catching the coincidental-average cutover case and does not — it fires only when the attributed quantity exceeds the matched tier's booked units, so an averaged draw that fits inside that tier passes both runtime nets and is closed by the barrier and the quiet gate alone; the worked example is now in the header. The quiet gate dropped its `xact_start <= now()` filter, which was a superset of the dangerous set only under an unenforced assumption that this transaction began after the barrier committed — it now refuses on any other open client-backend transaction and reports age via `clock_timestamp()`. Two guards added and mutation-tested: `DRAW_DOWN_CUTOVER_PREPARED_XACT` (prepared two-phase transactions never appear in `pg_stat_activity`; with a ghost present the backend scan read zero, confirming the blind spot empirically) and `DRAW_DOWN_CUTOVER_NOT_IN_TRANSACTION`, which asserts `lock_timeout` reads back `15s` so a non-transactional apply cannot silently no-op the whole cutover handshake. The bundling check was changed to `IS NOT FALSE` so a NULL reads as refusal, and its top-level-xid subtransaction gap is now recorded rather than implied. Also disclosed: 15s bounds each lock acquisition (~45s worst case, and the figure is unmeasured), and the draw-refusal window spans the `quote_items` CHECK validation, accepted rather than split into a third ordered migration. Re-proven end to end on PostgreSQL 17.10 against a fixture reproducing both live body md5s exactly: separate committed applies succeed with both postflight notices; a bundled apply is refused and rolls back with the wrapper still at its pre-barrier md5; a concurrent transaction, a prepared transaction, and a mutated `lock_timeout` are each refused by name, and each control run succeeds once the condition is cleared. Twelfth pass (push-proof, 2026-08-16, verdict BLOCKERS — one High): CRX-MONEY-TIER-ROUND-001. Every earlier pass had missed it, because it only shows up on FRACTIONAL quantities. The loop rounded each draw's extension in isolation, so on a booking drawn in several partial pieces the per-draw rounding residual accumulated instead of cancelling; the reported case books $1.00 as half a unit at $0.50 plus half a unit at $1.50 and, drawn as four quarter-unit draws, billed $1.02. Both premises were re-verified against current source before accepting the finding: the draw quantity box and the quote-line quantity boxes are all `step="any"`, so fractional draws are a real production input shape, not hypothetical. Fixed by rounding each tier's RUNNING TOTAL and billing the difference — the line owes `ROUND(price*(prior+take),2) - ROUND(price*prior,2)`, where `prior` is a new tier-CTE column holding the units already billed at that tier key — so successive draws telescope and the lines written against a tier sum to exactly `ROUND(price*units_drawn,2)` no matter how the draw was split. Cost uses the same form. Proven in-engine on PostgreSQL 17.10: the reported case now bills exactly $1.00 against $1.02 before; across twelve tier/draw shapes the new form is exact 12 of 12 where the old was exact 3 of 12 with a worst-case 9-cent error; and on four whole-unit shapes the new form is identical to the old, so the ordinary non-fractional draw is unchanged. The header's blanket "money is exact by construction rather than exact by rounding" claim was overstated for fractional quantities and has been narrowed to the property actually guaranteed, with the earlier wording flagged as a draft error. Both migrations re-applied clean in order on a fresh fixture whose pre-apply body hashes match the live pins exactly. NOT verified at that point: a full end-to-end draw through the live function, because the throwaway fixture carried only 7 of the ~12 tables that function touches — the twelfth-pass proof covered the changed arithmetic and the migration's own guards, not the surrounding call path. Thirteenth pass (push-proof, 2026-08-16, verdict BLOCKERS — two High) closed both that gap and the two new findings. CRX-MONEY-LIFECYCLE-001: telescoping on surviving UNITS is exact going forward but not path-independent through a reversal, because the subtrahend `ROUND(price*prior,2)` is a recomputed figure while the money standing on the surviving lines is whatever those lines were actually written at. Two identical quarter-unit draws at $0.50 write $0.13 and $0.12; voiding the first and redrawing the same quantity then billed $0.24, while voiding the second billed $0.25 — the same surviving quantity, two different bills, decided by which of two identical draws was reversed. Fixed by re-basing on the cents actually billed: the `billed` CTE gained a `money` column summing the surviving lines' own `total_price` (with the same cancelled-order branch the units column uses, so money and units always describe the same rows), and the line owes `GREATEST(ROUND(price*(prior+take),2) - money, 0)`. The `GREATEST` refuses to issue a silent credit — a credit belongs in a credit memo, a negative `total_price` would be refused by the whole-cent CHECKs anyway, and the quantity form of the same condition is already surfaced and refused by `DRAW_TIER_OVERCONSUMED`. Measured in-engine on PostgreSQL 17: path-independent where the units basis was not, exact in 36 of 36 void/redraw cases (worst error 0.00) against 26 of 36 for the units basis and 8 of 36 for the original per-draw form, and identical to the original form on all four whole-unit shapes. CRX-MONEY-PROFIT-001: a regression introduced by the twelfth-pass fix itself. Making the COST side cumulative desynchronised the header from the lines, because the canonical `_round_money_to_whole_cents` trigger (`20260809230500`) always overwrites `order_items.profit` with `total_price - ROUND(cost_per_unit * total_units_needed, 2)` and discards any caller-supplied profit, so a cumulative cost basis reached the header and the commission basis but never the stored lines.
